planting.note: Plant container-grown rosettes or offsets in spring in lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; this selected form of broadleaf stonecrop was collected near the Oregon coast for its unusually heavy silver-white farina coating.

directions: Plant offsets or small divisions in spring in lean, rocky, sharply drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, since heavy or waterlogged ground causes the tight rosettes to rot at the base. Cape Blanco carries an exceptionally dense coating of chalky white farina over its small, spoon-shaped, silver-blue leaves, giving a frostier, more silvered look than the species and a striking contrast against darker-leaved companions. Clusters of small bright yellow, star-shaped flowers rise just above the foliage mat in late spring, though the plant is grown chiefly for its year-round foliage color rather than its bloom. Once established it tolerates drought, thin soil, and coastal exposure with ease, making it a dependable choice for rock gardens, trough plantings, and green roofs; lift and replant loose rosettes every few years to keep the mat from thinning in the center.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Purpureum takes on its richest plum-purple foliage tones when grown lean and given plenty of direct sun.

directions: Plant divisions or rooted offsets in spring in lean, sharply drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade. Purpureum forms the same flattened, spoon-leaved rosettes as the species but overlays the silvery farina with deep plum-purple pigment that intensifies in cold weather and strong light, fading to a more muted purple-gray during summer heat or in shadier spots. Small clusters of bright yellow star-shaped flowers open just above the foliage in late spring, providing a vivid color contrast against the dark rosettes. It spreads slowly into a tight, low mat well suited to rock crevices, gravel gardens, and container plantings, and rarely needs more than an occasional light watering once its roots are established; divide congested clumps in spring if the center begins to thin.

common_name: Aureum Golden Moss Stonecrop (Yellow-Tipped Biting Stonecrop)

planting.note: Plant small cuttings or divisions in spring in very well-drained, lean, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; the golden new growth of 'Aureum' colors up brightest in poor, dry soil and strong light.

directions: Plant cuttings or small divisions in spring in lean, sandy or rocky, sharply drained soil in full sun, where poor fertility and dry conditions produce the tightest growth and brightest color. Aureum forms the same tiny, tightly packed, cylindrical leaves as the species but tips each new shoot in bright golden-yellow through spring and early summer, an effect that fades toward chartreuse-green as the foliage matures and temperatures rise. Masses of small, star-shaped yellow flowers cover the mat in early summer, briefly making the whole planting glow gold. It roots readily from broken stem fragments, making it easy to establish on green roofs, dry rock walls, and gravel paths where little else will grow; shear lightly after bloom if a tighter mat is wanted.

common_name: Bronze Carpet Stonecrop (Purple-Bronze Foliage Two-Row Sedum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted stem cuttings in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Bronze Carpet develops its deepest bronze-purple color when grown in full sun.

directions: Plant divisions or rooted stem cuttings in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, though color and flowering are best with more direct sun. Bronze Carpet spreads by trailing stems into a dense mat of rounded, fleshy leaves that deepen from green to a rich bronze-purple through the growing season, especially as nights cool in fall. Flat clusters of small starry pink flowers cover the mat in mid to late summer, drawing bees and butterflies over an extended bloom period. Like other two-row stonecrops it roots wherever a stem touches soil, making it fast and forgiving to establish along walls, slopes, and border edges, and tolerant of heat, drought, and poor soil once settled in; shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat tidy and encourage denser new growth.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Stardust declines in rich, wet soil, which causes floppy stems and reduced flowering just as it does in other showy stonecrops.

directions: Plant in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; excellent drainage keeps the thick, succulent stems from rotting over winter. Stardust bears the same broccoli-like flower buds and pale blue-green foliage typical of showy stonecrop, but opens to clean, pure white flower clusters rather than the pink to rose tones of Autumn Joy and most other spectabile selections, giving it a cooler, brighter presence in the late-summer border. Its sturdy, upright stems hold the flower heads well without staking, and the flat-topped clusters attract large numbers of bees and butterflies during the several weeks they remain open. The seedheads dry to a soft tan and can be left standing for winter interest; divide clumps every three to four years in spring as they become congested.

common_name: Autumn Charm Stonecrop (Variegated Cream-Edged Autumn Joy Sport)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; some shelter from the hottest afternoon sun helps preserve the crisp cream leaf margins of this variegated sport through summer.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, giving some protection from the most intense midday sun where summers are hot, which helps keep the variegation crisp rather than scorched. A sport of the classic Autumn Joy lineage, Autumn Charm carries the same blue-green, succulent leaves broadly edged in creamy white, turning the whole clump into a season-long foliage feature well before the flower buds ever form. Flat clusters of dusty pink flowers open in late summer and age to bronze-red, following the same color progression as its parent, though slightly shorter and more compact in habit. Watch for any shoots that revert to solid green and remove them promptly at the base, since reverted growth is more vigorous and will eventually overtake the variegated stems if left in place; divide every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Picolette's naturally dwarf, tight habit needs no pinching or staking to stay compact.

directions: Plant in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; lean conditions keep this naturally dwarf selection tight and sturdy without any pinching or staking. Picolette forms a dense, rounded mound of thick, dusky purple-green foliage noticeably smaller in every dimension than Autumn Joy and most other border stonecrops, making it well suited to the front of a border, a rock garden, or a container where larger upright sedums would overwhelm the space. Flat clusters of rich pink flowers open in late summer just above the foliage mound and age to a deeper rose as they mature. Its compact size means it rarely needs division for size control, though clumps can be split every few years in spring to propagate or renew vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; Angelina's Teacup holds its gold foliage color best with plenty of direct sun and lean, dry conditions.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, since rich or consistently moist ground softens the plant's compact form and mutes its foliage color. A SunSparkler-series hybrid tracing back to the popular groundcover Sedum rupestre 'Angelina', Angelina's Teacup keeps needle-like golden foliage through the growing season but forms a distinctly low, rounded mound rather than a sprawling mat, with the gold picking up rose-orange tints in cool fall weather. Clusters of soft pink flowers open above the foliage in late summer, giving a color combination unusual among gold-leaved sedums. Its dense, tidy habit fits neatly along a border edge, rock garden, or container without spreading aggressively; divide clumps in spring every few years to propagate or refresh an aging planting.

common_name: Blue Pillow Stonecrop (Powder-Blue Mounding SunSparkler Sedum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; Blue Pillow's powder-blue foliage color is most vivid in lean, dry conditions with plenty of direct light.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, avoiding rich or wet ground that softens this cultivar's tight habit and dulls its foliage color. A SunSparkler-series hybrid, Blue Pillow builds a dense, symmetrical dome of small, rounded, powder-blue leaves with a light frosty bloom, holding its color and shape from spring through fall better than many older blue-leaved sedums. Clusters of soft pink, star-shaped flowers appear above the mound in late summer, though the plant is grown primarily for its neat, cushion-like foliage form. Its compact, non-spreading habit makes it a dependable edging or container plant that rarely needs grooming beyond removing the occasional spent flower stem; divide in spring every few years to propagate.

common_name: Jade Tuffet Stonecrop (Dense Rounded Green-Leaved SunSparkler Sedum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Jade Tuffet keeps its dense, rounded shape without pinching or shearing.

directions: Plant in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; this SunSparkler-series selection tolerates a bit more shade than most gold- and blue-leaved sedums in the group without losing its tight form. Jade Tuffet forms an unusually dense, perfectly rounded mound of small, glossy, deep jade-green leaves, giving it a clipped, tuffet-like appearance without any pruning. Clusters of small pink flowers open above the foliage dome in late summer, drawing bees and butterflies, though the plant's chief appeal is its neat green form, which holds up well through summer heat and humidity. Its compact, well-behaved habit suits the front of a border, a rock garden, or a mixed container; divide clumps in spring every few years to propagate or renew vigor.
